At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for payments work on ACCESS Next Generation from **August 2009** to **June 2012**. The bank was consolidating regional treasury systems into a global corporate banking portal, but Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform needed custom engineering. Payment types had different formatting, validation, compliance, and approval requirements. Regional systems also had different data models and entitlement structures, while live payments had to continue uninterrupted.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, coordinating with bank stakeholders in Chicago and NY/NJ. He worked with enterprise architects, security specialists, regional compliance officers, and developers to determine where WebSeries’ native capabilities ended and bank-specific development was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, alongside Message Authentication Code security and payment-type-specific permissions. He also designed the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. For administrators, he replaced individual permission configuration with role-based profiles and bulk changes across users, accounts, and products, reducing entitlement management from **days to minutes**.

Matt led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. He coordinated regional launches around regulatory readiness rather than a single global deployment, and owned production incident response, cross-team root-cause analysis, status updates, and daily leadership calls.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. The gateway gave corporate treasurers a single entry point for payments across regions, replacing fragmented regional integrations.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. Most engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He focused on removing those barriers: psychological safety so people could speak honestly, decisions pushed to the people closest to the work, and engineering practices that gave teams confidence in what they shipped.

He makes intent explicit, uses transparency and direct feedback, and coaches teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, that included a “permit to fail” learning environment. Teams had avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than finger-pointing, and supported lean, low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. Teams applied those lessons to subsequent sprints to prevent repeat failures.

He also built balanced teams with engineers, product managers, and UX architects participating equally and sharing accountability for outcomes. Instead of hierarchical handoffs between separate functions, he embedded pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and real-time feedback into daily work. Teams could voice concerns and implement changes autonomously.

In innovation work, Matt set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail, intentionally. He used user research, JTBD framing, and rapid testing to validate assumptions before committing to costly builds.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. His balanced-team work also achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

🐾 Here’s what Matt has built and delivered.

Matt’s work spans Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement. At **Accenture**, clients were struggling with slow development cycles, fragmented workflows, and legacy systems. They wanted to move from waterfall and feature factories to iterative, customer-centric product development, but that meant changing how product managers, designers, and engineers worked together, not just introducing new tools.

Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, with full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and career development. He adapted Lean XP for enterprise compliance, security, and legacy systems. Instead of siloed functions handing work off, he established balanced teams combining product, engineering, and design. Instead of leaving quality to a separate QA phase, teams used pair programming, test-driven development, and automated pipelines.

At **Capital One**, slow, misaligned product iterations were extending time-to-market. Matt introduced a client-prioritized, testable backlog and disciplined red-green-refactor: write a failing test, write minimal code to pass it, then safely refactor. The **8-person** team delivered features **3 to 4x faster** than other **Accenture** teams on the same engagement, with **zero production defects**. **Capital One** sought to retain the team beyond the planned end.

He also built the training behind delivery. New hires who lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience progressed through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model, supported by mentors and tailored training. The centers achieved near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**.

Across the centers, teams delivered **30+ product engagements** for **15+ Fortune 500 clients**. Delivery excellence and customer relationship building generated **\$100M+ in repeat business**, and client teams continued using the practices after engagements ended.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation instead of verifying it. He focused on delivery pressures without confirming access patterns, auditing who could trigger downstream email processes, or verifying that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed. Afterward, IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.”
